NOTE: I haven't finished writing or implemented all of these rules in my projects just yet.

## NAMESPACING:

I use triple namespacing with affixes: `project_name.api`, `project_name.internal`, `command.project_name`.

- `api` namespace contains a stable api surface within the project major version, for external use.
- `internal` is for the code that should not be touched directly from the outside, which is the majority of the code, and is subject to frequent random changes.
- `command` is for functions that are meant to be used by the player like a normal command. These are also provided via a chat based interactive GUI (fully custom icons, composable from data packs - in text components. There's a lot of naming and organization patterns, so I won't write it all out here. Still partially WIP though).

As opposed to others, `command` is a prefix, to group all the related end-used-facing functions across projects together for easier access for players in chat.

I don't use abbreviations for namespaces, and avoid them in general.

## MAIN STRUCTURE:

I organize code within top-level (directly inside "function" dir, etc.) directories, each relating to a feature `module`, such as `animation`, `item`, `effect`, `cooldown`...
Modules are self enclosed specialized systems.

I run all my tick code from a 2 `@a` and a single `@e` selector and heavily rely on `@s` checks throughout my projects.
I try to avoid selectors other that `@s` as much as possible.

Next to those top-level module dirs, there are also:

- `core`: main data pack non-content structure: load, tick, etc.
- `util`: random reusable utilities
- `data`: general data initialization and handling for scoreboards, storage, constants
- `config`: anything regarding data pack configuration
- `error`: error handling system (mainly for api io)

I group related execution paths and terminate early with `if score`, `if entity @s[tag=<...>]`, etc.

## FUNCTION NAMING:

When relevant I use these naming pattern for functions, and directories, in which case the meaning applies to all contenst of the dir:

- `_m` postfix - macro
- `if_` prefix - returns a success state for the stated condition to be used in the `execute if function` command chain.
- `if_<...>_then_<...>`, same as `if_` but when the condition is met, also performs another action. Still returns the success of the condition.
- `if_<...>_else_<...>`, same as above but the extra action takes place when the condition is not met.
- `get_` prefix - returns some sort of data, by setting a specific scoreboard or data storage value.

## DATA:

I namespace all scoreboards and scoreboard tags (`/tag` command). Same with top level object in custom data components. These namespaces include the sub-namespace (`project_name.api`, etc).

I type all my data with mcdoc, and make it extensible for relevant api data.
I validate type (and contents when possible) of data incomming via the api.

I build optional api systems to be only enabled by other projects during load time. These auto disable themselves. This avoids developers not disabling them, or other data packs being removed by the player without running the cleanup first.

## COMPATIBILITY:

I maintain the main `data` dir with the code for the version supported by the pack (for multi version packs), and add backwards compatibility fixes in overlays. An example overlay name is: `compat_until_	1_21_10` (inclusive), a lower bound would be `since_x_y_z`.

I always strive to make my data packs fully featured for all environments: single/multi-player, hardcore, except peaceful mode. All the content needs to be accessible in all cases, but peaceful.

## HAVE A NICE DAY!

This is all for a WIP data pack framework (itself a data pack).

Feel free to ask more on discord: `rafalberezin`.

Also, I want to solve Advent of Code (2015) with data packs. Due to lack of time I completed first 3 days so far and have a break from minecraft (so I might have forgot or misremembered something here too).

There are quite a few methods specific to mcfunction, for example giving the current entity an INIT tag on summon so you can modify / position it correctly with commands.

A player ID system (or player specific storage) is also extremely useful. Raycasting (or recursion in general), Implementing custom blocks is quite unique... 

The fact that we use quite a lot of workarounds to accomplish what we want. A great example is using advancements as an event based trigger.

The way we optimize entity selectors is also quite interesting. 

Mcfunction doesn't have propper version resolution so we implement something like lantern load so we can propperly load libraries.

Mcfunction is also a very repetetive language. For example displaying an animation (progress bar or some notification...) using custom font charracters is usually a long file filled with score checks.
column25:
Many features are lacking, for example we can't add propper items / custom blocks in a freaking block game :P A way to get the current time would also be nice. And a propper way to do version resolution. Managing an inventory or just rendering any hud is pretty difficult

There are also a lot of things that are technically possible but are quite annoying to do. For example we don't have something like a for loop or a while loop. 

There is no way to handle events. Implementing async functions (through the schedule command) looses all it's context so keepting that is also pretty annoying. 

Implementing a simple wait can be quite annoying too since you'd need to add a scoreboard and increment it every time. 

Many times you want to run multiple commands within the same context. This requires you to create a new mcfunction file and that's why we end up with 20 different file. Naming all of those files is also a night mare since well, they all need to be different.

Multilining is also very annoying since you have to place a backslash after each line

Overall the performance of selectors and data commands is very bad. This means we have to optimize as much as we can if we're making anything remotely close to a big datapack.

Datapacks aren't very compatable with eachother. for example there is only one actionbar to display some hud elements and there is no way to manage any priority. Editing minecraft-related code with a datapack also ruins performance. This can be as simple as adding an item to a loot table from a mob.




Anyways I hope this helps you, have a nice day and good luck with your paper!

the general pattern that i dislike about mcfunction is the simplicity of it. its wayyy too simple sometimes!

like when it comes to how it handles math with scoreboard operations. its actually awfully similar to assembly! following, is a valid assembly code with comments that describe the operations. 

mov eax, 10  ; eax = 10
mov ebx, eax ; ebx = eax

add eax, ebx ; eax += ebx
sub eax, ebx ; eax -= ebx
mul eax, ebx ; eax *= ebx
div eax, ebx ; eax /= ebx

isnt that awfully familiar? yes, because that is EXACTLY how you do math with scoreboards!
mcfunction is just too explicit, too simple, it is in a way similar assembly where you only have a specific set of the simplest instructions. nothing too complex.

yes, you could build infinitely complex logic with those simple instructions. but the problem is that if complexity is not in the language, then it is in the source code. you pretty much cant do anything directly. if-else chains use workarounds with a boolean variable, for/while loops use recursive functions, array iteration is slightly complicated recursive algorithm. for example, the following is pseudo code of array iteration implementation

- check first array element [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
    - if first element > 3 replace with 0
- append the first array element to this same array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 1]
- remove the first array element [2, 3, 4, 5, 1]
- repeat until array over

thats how you do it. and when a language is THAT simple, adding a little abstraction over it would really help in development productivity and readability, which also means easier debugging and mental overhead! that was the short answer, to the question of "what i dislike about mcfunction"

column25: As a programmer outside datapacks, it is weird how things which should be easy in ordinary programming are difficult in datapacks. Loops are one of the pillars of any other programming language, and yet mcfunction has to use recursion? Schedule is kind of like a sleep function, but you have to work around context not being preserved? Why is doing scoreboard calculations a multi-step process (literally math, the thing computers do)? It's obvious it wasn't designed as a programming language, only acquired the strictly necessary features over time. As a result, we have a language where some low-level features just don't exist and are papered over with janky high-level implementations. I'm reminded of hijacking various features of loot tables, predicates, item modifiers, or so forth to implement certain things entirely unrelated to their intended purpose, such as implementing randomness before /random became vanilla. It's just foundationally very interesting, even taken apart from all the vanilla Minecraft features that are hard to implement (/motion please.........) Anyway, thanks for putting up with my yap and best the luck on your university project!

I am working on making three datapacks right now:
- A port of Slimefun4
- My own datapack library to make it possible (and hopefully easy) to add custom items, recipes, multiblocks, etc.
- A datapack that will contain and deploy a mining server with light rouge-lite elements

The Slimefun4 (Sf4) port and my library, Eseframe, are being developed in parallel. The project started as a spiritual successor which would be my own take on Sf4 for balanced around survival mode. Eventually, though, I decided to split the logic and the content into separate packs. I still want to make that successor in the future, but I decided first I just want to focus on making a library and pack that is capable of matching Sf4.

At that point I generally knew that library is existing, and even though I hadn't checked, I knew there probably might be a library like this already, but i decided I was going to build everything in it from the ground up to gain experience in development.

That's also the reason I started using Git, and then later on, GitHub. Even though things like Smithed exist already, and could potentially be objectively better at it'sintended purpose, i decided that the best way to really know how these libraries work is to make my own.

Even if I don't end up using Eseframe, it will have given me valuable experience with Git, GitHub, SSH (I almost lost the project once so I set up a NAS after getting it back), and writing documentation.

After actually looking into the Smithed ecosystem a bit, i came to the conclusion that their libraries are different enough from Eseframe to justify its existence:
- While Smith is embedded and is under MIT, Eseframe is meant to be put directly into the datapacks folder as the single source of truth, and is under LGPL v3
- Smithed libraries are technical and focused on a specific mechanic, Eseframe is made to be user-friendly and easy to work with (you can read the docs from ingame!), even with little experience.
I've decided that once I have finalized the syntax for the API (which I version numbered like some Smithed libraries do to keep things backwards-compatible) and finish cleaning up my code, I am going to do two things:
1. I'll start work on a Smithed compatibility update. Not like a full refactor, but just some things to comply to compatibility standards like checking for safety tags.
2. I'm gonna lean further into the user friendliness by making an ingame item/recipe editor

As for conventions, I don't really have formal conventions written down, but I've made my own over time:
- The API and internal logic use different namespaces
